/-!
# Discrete logarithms on elliptic curves in sub-exponential time

Let $E$ be an elliptic curve over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$, let $P \in E(\mathbb{F}_q)$ and
let $Q \in \langle P \rangle$. The *elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem* asks for an
integer $k$ with $Q = kP$. Wikipedia's list of unsolved problems in mathematics asks:

> Can a discrete logarithm on an elliptic curve be computed in sub-exponential time?

Here "sub-exponential" means time $2^{o(n)}$, where $n$ is the bit-length of the input
(which is proportional to $\log q$). The best known classical algorithms for general elliptic
curves (Pollard's rho, baby-step giant-step) take time $q^{1/2 + o(1)} = 2^{\Theta(n)}$.

* The model of computation is the deterministic Turing machine `Turing.FinTM2` from Mathlib,
  with worst-case running time, as in the formalisation of P vs NP in this repository
  (`FormalConjectures/Millenium/PvsNP.lean`). Randomised algorithms with expected running
  time bounds are not covered. Quantum algorithms are not covered.
* The input is a tuple of natural numbers `DiscreteLogarithm2.Input`. The finite field
  $\mathbb{F}_q = \mathbb{F}_p[X]/(f)$ is given by the prime $p$ and an irreducible polynomial
  $f$; polynomials and field elements are given by their base-$p$ digits. Every finite field
  arises in this way. Curves are given by general Weierstrass coefficients
  $a_1, a_2, a_3, a_4, a_6$ (so that characteristics $2$ and $3$ are covered), and points by
  affine coordinates or a flag for the point at infinity.

  proportional to $\log q$ for canonical inputs. This is the encoding
  `DiscreteLogarithm2.Input.finEncoding`. The notion of time $2^{o(n)}$ is invariant under
  changing the encoding or the machine model by polynomial factors.

  is a valid instance (with $Q \in \langle P \rangle$); its output on other inputs is arbitrary.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Discrete logarithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/discrete_logarithm)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [Wikipedia, Elliptic-curve cryptography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic-curve_cryptography)

namespace DiscreteLogarithm2

/- ### A binary encoding of lists of natural numbers -/

/-- Encode a list of natural numbers over the alphabet `Option Bool`: every entry is written in
binary (using `Computability.encodeNat`) and followed by the separator `none`. -/
def encodeListNat (l : List ℕ) : List (Option Bool) :=
  l.flatMap fun n => (encodeNat n).map some ++ [none]

/-- Decode a word over `Option Bool` to a list of natural numbers by splitting it at the
separators `none`. This is a left inverse of `encodeListNat`. -/
def decodeListNat (l : List (Option Bool)) : List ℕ :=
  (l.splitOnP Option.isNone).dropLast.map fun w => decodeNat (w.map (·.getD false))

@[simp, category API, AMS 68]
theorem decode_encodeListNat : ∀ l : List ℕ, decodeListNat (encodeListNat l) = l
  | [] => rfl
  | n :: l => by
    have ih := decode_encodeListNat l
    simp only [decodeListNat, encodeListNat, List.flatMap_cons, List.append_assoc,
      List.singleton_append] at ih ⊢
    rw [splitOnP_append_cons _ _ _ _ rfl, splitOnP_isNone_map_some, List.singleton_append,
      List.dropLast_cons_of_ne_nil (List.splitOnP_ne_nil _ _), List.map_cons, ih]
    simp

@[category test, AMS 68]
theorem decodeListNat_example :
    decodeListNat [some true, none, some false, some true, none, none] = [1, 2, 0] := by
  decide

/-- The binary encoding of `List ℕ` over the alphabet `Option Bool` given by `encodeListNat`.
The length of the encoding of `l` is the sum over `l` of the binary lengths of its entries plus
`l.length`. -/
def finEncodingListNat : FinEncoding (List ℕ) where
  Γ := Option Bool
  encode := encodeListNat
  decode l := some (decodeListNat l)
  decode_encode l := by simp
  ΓFin := inferInstance

/- ### Instances of the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem -/

/-- The input to the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem, as a tuple of natural numbers.

A natural number `n` is interpreted as the polynomial over `ZMod p`, or the element of
$\mathbb{F}_p[X]/(f)$, whose coefficients are the base-`p` digits of `n`. Not every `Input` is a
valid instance, see `DiscreteLogarithm2.IsSolver` for the validity conditions. -/
structure Input where
  /-- The characteristic `p` of the finite field. -/
  p : ℕ
  /-- The polynomial `f` over `ZMod p` defining the field $\mathbb{F}_q = \mathbb{F}_p[X]/(f)$. -/
  f : ℕ
  /-- The Weierstrass coefficient $a_1$. -/
  a₁ : ℕ
  /-- The Weierstrass coefficient $a_2$. -/
  a₂ : ℕ
  /-- The Weierstrass coefficient $a_3$. -/
  a₃ : ℕ
  /-- The Weierstrass coefficient $a_4$. -/
  a₄ : ℕ
  /-- The Weierstrass coefficient $a_6$. -/
  a₆ : ℕ
  /-- The point `P`: `none` is the point at infinity, `some (x, y)` an affine point. -/
  P : Option (ℕ × ℕ)
  /-- The point `Q`: `none` is the point at infinity, `some (x, y)` an affine point. -/
  Q : Option (ℕ × ℕ)

/-- Encode a possibly infinite point as three natural numbers: a flag and two coordinates. -/
def encodePoint : Option (ℕ × ℕ) → List ℕ
  | none => [0, 0, 0]
  | some (x, y) => [1, x, y]

/-- Decode a flag and two coordinates to a possibly infinite point. -/

  if b = 0 then none else some (x, y)

def Input.toList (i : Input) : List ℕ :=
  [i.p, i.f, i.a₁, i.a₂, i.a₃, i.a₄, i.a₆] ++ encodePoint i.P ++ encodePoint i.Q

/-- Read an input from a list of `13` natural numbers. -/
def Input.ofList : List ℕ → Option Input
  | [p, f, a₁, a₂, a₃, a₄, a₆, bP, xP, yP, bQ, xQ, yQ] =>
    some ⟨p, f, a₁, a₂, a₃, a₄, a₆, decodePoint bP xP yP, decodePoint bQ xQ yQ⟩
  | _ => none

@[simp, category API, AMS 68]
theorem Input.ofList_toList (i : Input) : Input.ofList i.toList = some i := by
  rcases i with ⟨p, f, a₁, a₂, a₃, a₄, a₆, _ | ⟨xP, yP⟩, _ | ⟨xQ, yQ⟩⟩ <;>
    simp [Input.toList, Input.ofList, encodePoint, decodePoint]

/-- The binary encoding of inputs: the `13` natural numbers of `Input.toList` are encoded with
`encodeListNat`. The length of the encoding of `i` is the sum of the binary lengths of the `13`
numbers in `i.toList` plus `13`. For a valid instance over $\mathbb{F}_q$ whose field elements
are given by numbers less than $q$, this is $\Theta(\log q)$. -/
def Input.finEncoding : FinEncoding Input where
  Γ := finEncodingListNat.Γ
  encode i := finEncodingListNat.encode i.toList
  decode l := (finEncodingListNat.decode l).bind Input.ofList
  decode_encode i := by simp [finEncodingListNat]
  ΓFin := finEncodingListNat.ΓFin

/-- The polynomial over `ZMod p` whose coefficients are the base-`p` digits of `n`. -/
noncomputable def natToPoly (p n : ℕ) : (ZMod p)[X] :=
  Nat.ofDigits X (Nat.digits p n)

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem natToPoly_five_seven : natToPoly 5 7 = 2 + X := by
  norm_num [natToPoly, Nat.ofDigits]

/-- The element of $\mathbb{F}_p[X]/(f)$ whose coefficients, in the powers of the root of `f`,
are the base-`p` digits of `n`. -/
noncomputable def natToAdjoinRoot {p : ℕ} (f : (ZMod p)[X]) (n : ℕ) : AdjoinRoot f :=
  Nat.ofDigits (AdjoinRoot.root f) (Nat.digits p n)

@[category API, AMS 11]
theorem map_ofDigits {R S : Type*} [Semiring R] [Semiring S] (φ : R →+* S) (b : R)
    (L : List ℕ) : φ (Nat.ofDigits b L) = Nat.ofDigits (φ b) L := by
  induction L with
  | nil => simp [Nat.ofDigits]
  | cons d L ih => simp [Nat.ofDigits, ih]

@[category API, AMS 11]
theorem natToAdjoinRoot_eq {p : ℕ} (f : (ZMod p)[X]) (n : ℕ) :
    natToAdjoinRoot f n = AdjoinRoot.mk f (natToPoly p n) := by
  rw [natToPoly, natToAdjoinRoot, map_ofDigits, AdjoinRoot.mk_X]

/-- The polynomial `f` over `ZMod p` given by an input. -/
noncomputable def Input.modulus (i : Input) : (ZMod i.p)[X] :=
  natToPoly i.p i.f

/-- The ring $\mathbb{F}_p[X]/(f)$ given by an input. This is the field $\mathbb{F}_q$ with
$q = p^{\deg f}$ when `p` is prime and `f` is irreducible. -/
abbrev Input.Field (i : Input) : Type :=
  AdjoinRoot i.modulus

/-- The Weierstrass curve over $\mathbb{F}_p[X]/(f)$ given by an input. -/
noncomputable def Input.curve (i : Input) : WeierstrassCurve.Affine i.Field where
  a₁ := natToAdjoinRoot i.modulus i.a₁
  a₂ := natToAdjoinRoot i.modulus i.a₂
  a₃ := natToAdjoinRoot i.modulus i.a₃
  a₄ := natToAdjoinRoot i.modulus i.a₄
  a₆ := natToAdjoinRoot i.modulus i.a₆

/-- `i.IsPointRepr o P` says that the raw data `o` of the input `i` represents the point `P` of
the curve of `i`: `none` represents the point at infinity and `some (x, y)` represents the
affine point with coordinates given by `x` and `y`. -/
def Input.IsPointRepr (i : Input) : Option (ℕ × ℕ) → i.curve.Point → Prop
  | none, P => P = 0
  | some (x, y), P => ∃ h : i.curve.Nonsingular (natToAdjoinRoot i.modulus x)
      (natToAdjoinRoot i.modulus y), P = .some h

open scoped Classical in
/-- A function `sol : Input → ℕ` solves the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem if
`sol i • P = Q` for every input `i` that is a valid instance. An input is a valid instance if
* `p` is prime and `f` is irreducible over `ZMod p`, so that $\mathbb{F}_q = \mathbb{F}_p[X]/(f)$
  is a finite field,
* the Weierstrass curve $E$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ is an elliptic curve, i.e. its discriminant is
  nonzero,
* the raw data for `P` and `Q` represent points $P, Q \in E(\mathbb{F}_q)$, and
* $Q$ lies in the subgroup generated by $P$.

Nothing is required of `sol` on inputs that are not valid instances. -/
def IsSolver (sol : Input → ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ (i : Input) (hp : i.p.Prime) (hf : Irreducible i.modulus),
    haveI := Fact.mk hp
    haveI := Fact.mk hf
    ∀ (_ : i.curve.IsElliptic) (P Q : i.curve.Point),
      i.IsPointRepr i.P P → i.IsPointRepr i.Q Q → Q ∈ AddSubgroup.zmultiples P →
        sol i • P = Q

/- ### Sub-exponential time -/

/-- A function `f : α → β` is computable in sub-exponential time if there is a deterministic
Turing machine (`Turing.FinTM2`) computing `f`, with respect to the encodings `ea` and `eb`,
that halts on every input of length `n` within `T n` steps, where $T(n) = 2^{o(n)}$, i.e.
for every $\varepsilon > 0$ we have $T(n) \le 2^{\varepsilon n}$ for all large $n$. -/
def IsComputableInSubexponentialTime {α β : Type} (ea : FinEncoding α) (eb : FinEncoding β)
    (f : α → β) : Prop :=
  ∃ M : TM2ComputableInTime ea eb f,
    ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop, (M.time n : ℝ) ≤ 2 ^ (ε * n)

/-- **Elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem in sub-exponential time.**

Can a discrete logarithm on an elliptic curve be computed in sub-exponential time?

That is, is there a deterministic Turing machine which, given a prime $p$, an irreducible
polynomial $f$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$ defining $\mathbb{F}_q = \mathbb{F}_p[X]/(f)$, an elliptic

time on inputs of length $n$ is $2^{o(n)}$? Here $n$ is proportional to $\log q$. -/

    answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ sol : Input → ℕ, IsSolver sol ∧
      IsComputableInSubexponentialTime Input.finEncoding finEncodingNatBool sol := by
  sorry

/-- Interpret polynomial-basis coefficients in the extension defined by `f`. -/
noncomputable def fieldElement {p : ℕ} (f : (ZMod p)[X]) (a : ElementCode) : AdjoinRoot f :=
  AdjoinRoot.mk f (coefficientPolynomial p a)

/-- The Weierstrass curve described by an input code over its encoded field. -/
noncomputable def curve (c : InputCode) :
    WeierstrassCurve (AdjoinRoot (coefficientPolynomial c.p c.modulus)) :=
  let f := coefficientPolynomial c.p c.modulus
  ⟨fieldElement f c.a₁, fieldElement f c.a₂, fieldElement f c.a₃,
    fieldElement f c.a₄, fieldElement f c.a₆⟩

/-- `EncodesPoint f W s P` says that `s` is the polynomial-basis encoding of the point `P` on
`W`. -/
noncomputable def EncodesPoint {p : ℕ} (f : (ZMod p)[X]) [Fact (Irreducible f)]
    (W : WeierstrassCurve (AdjoinRoot f)) : PointCode → W.toAffine.Point → Prop
  | none, P => P = 0
  | some (x, y), P =>
      ∃ h : W.toAffine.Nonsingular (fieldElement f x) (fieldElement f y),
        P = WeierstrassCurve.Affine.Point.some h

/-- A self-delimiting binary encoding of a natural number. -/
def encodeNumber (n : ℕ) : List Bool :=
  let bits := Computability.encodeNat n
  List.replicate bits.length true ++ false :: bits

/-- A compact self-delimiting encoding of a list of natural numbers. -/
def encodeList (a : List ℕ) : List Bool :=
  encodeNumber a.length ++ a.flatMap encodeNumber

/-- A compact self-delimiting encoding of an affine point or the point at infinity. -/
def encodePoint : PointCode → List Bool
  | none => [false]
  | some (x, y) => true :: (encodeList x ++ encodeList y)

/-- The compact bitstring serialization of an elliptic-curve discrete-logarithm instance. -/
def serialize (c : InputCode) : List Bool :=
  encodeNumber c.p ++ encodeList c.modulus ++ encodeList c.a₁ ++ encodeList c.a₂ ++
    encodeList c.a₃ ++ encodeList c.a₄ ++ encodeList c.a₆ ++ encodePoint c.P ++ encodePoint c.Q

/-- `IsDiscreteLog c k` means that `c` describes an elliptic curve over a finite field, points
`P,Q` on it, and $Q=kP$.

The finite field is presented as $\mathbb F_p[X]/(f)$ with `p` prime and `f` monic irreducible.
Every finite field has such a presentation. -/
noncomputable def IsDiscreteLog (c : InputCode) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ hp : c.p.Prime,
    letI : Fact c.p.Prime := ⟨hp⟩
    let f := coefficientPolynomial c.p c.modulus
    f.Monic ∧ ∃ hf : Irreducible f,
      letI : Fact (Irreducible f) := ⟨hf⟩
      let W := curve c
      ∃ hW : W.IsElliptic,
        letI : W.IsElliptic := hW
        ∃ P Q : W.toAffine.Point,
          EncodesPoint f W c.P P ∧ EncodesPoint f W c.Q Q ∧ Q = k • P

/--
Can a discrete logarithm on an elliptic curve be computed in subexponential time?

Precisely, does there exist a deterministic classical Turing machine which, for every elliptic
curve over every finite field and every encoded pair $P,Q$ with $Q\in\langle P\rangle$, outputs
$k$ such that $Q=kP$? The running time is subexponential in the input bit-length $n$: its natural
logarithm is $o(n)$. Finite fields use prime-polynomial presentations, and the runtime is worst-case.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11 68]
theorem discrete_logarithm_2 :
    answer(sorry) ↔
      ∃ solve : List Bool → List Bool,
      ∃ A : TM2ComputableInTime finEncodingListBool finEncodingListBool solve,
        (fun n : ℕ ↦ Real.log (A.time n : ℝ)) =o[atTop] (fun n : ℕ ↦ (n : ℝ)) ∧
        ∀ c : InputCode, (∃ k, IsDiscreteLog c k) →
          IsDiscreteLog c (Computability.decodeNat (solve (serialize c))) := by
  sorry

end DiscreteLogarithm2

Allowed the output to be any natural k satisfying Q = k • P; uniqueness is neither required nor intended because discrete logarithms on finite groups are defined modulo the order of P.

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Discrete logarithms on elliptic curves

Let $E$ be an elliptic curve over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$, let $P$ be a point of $E$ and let
$Q$ be a point of the cyclic subgroup generated by $P$. The *elliptic curve discrete logarithm
problem* asks for an integer $k$ with $Q = kP$.

Wikipedia's list of unsolved problems in mathematics asks:

> Can a discrete logarithm on a elliptic curve be computed in sub-exponential time?

The best known classical algorithms for a general elliptic curve are generic algorithms such as
Pollard's rho method, which run in time exponential in the input size (about $\sqrt{q}$ group
operations).

We formalise the question as follows. An algorithm is a deterministic Turing machine (`FinTM2`
from Mathlib), and its running time is measured in the worst case as a function of the input
length, as in `TM2ComputableInTime`. Sub-exponential time means running time $2^{o(n)}$ in the
input length $n$; every $L_q[\alpha, c]$ bound with $\alpha < 1$ is of this form. The input
consists of a prime $p$, a polynomial $f \in \mathbb{F}_p[X]$ (which is required to be irreducible,
so that $\mathbb{F}_p[X]/(f)$ is the finite field of order $p^{\deg f}$; every finite field arises
in this way), the five Weierstrass coefficients of the curve, and the two points $P$ and $Q$.
Elements of the finite field are written as natural numbers whose base-$p$ digits are the
coefficients of a polynomial in the root of $f$. The algorithm must work for every elliptic
curve over every finite field, and must output $k \geq 0$ with $Q = kP$ whenever $Q$ lies in the
subgroup generated by $P$.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Discrete logarithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/discrete_logarithm)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [Wikipedia, Elliptic-curve cryptography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic-curve_cryptography)
- [Wikipedia, Time complexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_complexity#Sub-exponential_time)
- S. D. Galbraith and P. Gaudry, *Recent progress on the elliptic curve discrete logarithm
  problem*, Designs, Codes and Cryptography 78 (2016), 51–72.
-/

open Computability Turing Filter Polynomial

namespace DiscreteLogarithm2

/-- A time bound `t : ℕ → ℕ` is *sub-exponential* if `t n = 2 ^ o(n)`, that is, if for every
`ε > 0` we have `t n ≤ 2 ^ (ε * n)` for all sufficiently large `n`. -/
def IsSubexponential (t : ℕ → ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop, (t n : ℝ) ≤ 2 ^ (ε * n)

/-- Constant time is sub-exponential. -/
@[category test, AMS 68]
theorem isSubexponential_one : IsSubexponential fun _ => 1 := by
  intro ε hε
  filter_upwards with n
  simpa using Real.one_le_rpow one_le_two (mul_nonneg hε.le n.cast_nonneg)

/-- Exponential time is not sub-exponential. -/
@[category test, AMS 68]
theorem not_isSubexponential_two_pow : ¬ IsSubexponential (2 ^ ·) := by
  intro h
  obtain ⟨N, hN⟩ := (h (1 / 2) (by norm_num)).exists_forall_of_atTop
  have h1 : ((2 ^ max N 1 : ℕ) : ℝ) ≤ 2 ^ ((1 / 2 : ℝ) * (max N 1 : ℕ)) :=
    hN _ (le_max_left _ _)
  have h2 : (1 : ℝ) ≤ max N 1 := by exact_mod_cast le_max_right N 1
  have h3 : (2 : ℝ) ^ ((1 / 2 : ℝ) * (max N 1 : ℕ)) < 2 ^ ((max N 1 : ℕ) : ℝ) :=
    Real.rpow_lt_rpow_of_exponent_lt one_lt_two (by linarith)
  rw [Real.rpow_natCast] at h3
  rw [Nat.cast_pow, Nat.cast_ofNat] at h1
  linarith

/-- A binary encoding of lists of natural numbers over the alphabet `Option Bool`: every entry is
written in binary (using `encodeNat`) and is followed by the separator `none`. -/
def finEncodingListNat : FinEncoding (List ℕ) where
  Γ := Option Bool
  encode l := l.flatMap fun n => (encodeNat n).map some ++ [none]
  decode l :=
    some (((l.splitOnP Option.isNone).dropLast).map fun w => decodeNat (w.map (·.getD false)))
  decode_encode l := by
    have key : ∀ l : List ℕ,
        ((l.flatMap fun n => (encodeNat n).map some ++ [none]).splitOnP Option.isNone) =
          (l.map fun n => (encodeNat n).map some) ++ [[]] := by
      intro l
      induction l with
      | nil => simp
      | cons n l ih =>
        rw [List.flatMap_cons, List.append_assoc, List.singleton_append,
          List.splitOnP_first _ _ (fun x hx => by
            simp only [List.mem_map] at hx
            obtain ⟨b, -, rfl⟩ := hx
            simp) none rfl _,
          ih, List.map_cons, List.cons_append]
    simp [key, List.map_map, Function.comp_def]
  ΓFin := inferInstance

/-- The raw input of an instance of the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem, as a tuple of
natural numbers.

The finite field is `𝔽_p[X] / (f)`, where the coefficients of the polynomial `f` are the
base-`p` digits of the natural number `f` (least significant digit first). An element of this field is given by a
natural number whose base-`p` digits are the coefficients of a polynomial in the root of `f`.
Points are given by their affine coordinates, and `none` denotes the point at infinity. -/
structure Input where
  /-- The characteristic `p` of the finite field. -/
  p : ℕ
  /-- The base-`p` digits of `f` are the coefficients of the irreducible polynomial defining the
  finite field `𝔽_p[X] / (f)`. -/
  f : ℕ
  /-- The coefficient `a₁` of the Weierstrass equation. -/
  a₁ : ℕ
  /-- The coefficient `a₂` of the Weierstrass equation. -/
  a₂ : ℕ
  /-- The coefficient `a₃` of the Weierstrass equation. -/
  a₃ : ℕ
  /-- The coefficient `a₄` of the Weierstrass equation. -/
  a₄ : ℕ
  /-- The coefficient `a₆` of the Weierstrass equation. -/
  a₆ : ℕ
  /-- The base point `P`; `none` is the point at infinity. -/
  P : Option (ℕ × ℕ)
  /-- The point `Q` whose discrete logarithm with respect to `P` is sought; `none` is the point at
  infinity. -/
  Q : Option (ℕ × ℕ)

namespace Input

/-- Encoding of a point: the first entry is `0` for the point at infinity and `1` for an affine
point, and the next two entries are the coordinates. -/
def encodePoint : Option (ℕ × ℕ) → List ℕ
  | none => [0, 0, 0]
  | some (x, y) => [1, x, y]

/-- The input as a list of natural numbers. -/
def encode (I : Input) : List ℕ :=
  [I.p, I.f, I.a₁, I.a₂, I.a₃, I.a₄, I.a₆] ++ encodePoint I.P ++ encodePoint I.Q

/-- The encoding of an input always has `13` entries. -/
@[category test, AMS 68]
theorem length_encode (I : Input) : I.encode.length = 13 := by
  rcases I with ⟨p, f, a₁, a₂, a₃, a₄, a₆, _ | ⟨x, y⟩, _ | ⟨x', y'⟩⟩ <;> rfl

/-- Distinct inputs have distinct encodings. -/
@[category test, AMS 68]
theorem encode_injective : Function.Injective encode := by
  rintro ⟨p, f, a₁, a₂, a₃, a₄, a₆, _ | ⟨x, y⟩, _ | ⟨x', y'⟩⟩
    ⟨p', f', a₁', a₂', a₃', a₄', a₆', _ | ⟨z, w⟩, _ | ⟨z', w'⟩⟩ h <;>
  simp_all [encode, encodePoint]

/-- The polynomial `f ∈ 𝔽_p[X]` whose coefficients are the base-`p` digits of `I.f`. -/
noncomputable def modulus (I : Input) : (ZMod I.p)[X] :=
  Nat.ofDigits X (Nat.digits I.p I.f)

/-- The ring `𝔽_p[X] / (f)`; this is the finite field of order `p ^ deg f` when `p` is prime and
`f` is irreducible. -/
abbrev FiniteField (I : Input) : Type :=
  AdjoinRoot I.modulus

/-- The element of `𝔽_p[X] / (f)` whose base-`p` digits `c₀, c₁, …` are the coefficients of
the polynomial `c₀ + c₁ α + c₂ α² + ⋯` in the root `α` of `f`. -/
noncomputable def elem (I : Input) (c : ℕ) : I.FiniteField :=
  Nat.ofDigits (AdjoinRoot.root I.modulus) (Nat.digits I.p c)

/-- The Weierstrass curve `Y² + a₁XY + a₃Y = X³ + a₂X² + a₄X + a₆` over `𝔽_p[X] / (f)`
given by the input. -/
noncomputable def curve (I : Input) : WeierstrassCurve I.FiniteField where
  a₁ := I.elem I.a₁
  a₂ := I.elem I.a₂
  a₃ := I.elem I.a₃
  a₄ := I.elem I.a₄
  a₆ := I.elem I.a₆

/-- The nonsingular point `P` of the curve is the one described by the raw point data `r`: either
`r = none` and `P` is the point at infinity, or `r = some (x, y)` and `P` is the affine point with
coordinates given by `x` and `y`. -/
def IsPoint (I : Input) (r : Option (ℕ × ℕ)) (P : I.curve.toAffine.Point) : Prop :=
  match r with
  | none => P = 0
  | some (x, y) => ∃ h : I.curve.toAffine.Nonsingular (I.elem x) (I.elem y), P = .some h

end Input

/--
**Sub-exponential elliptic curve discrete logarithms.**

Can a discrete logarithm on an elliptic curve be computed in sub-exponential time?

That is, is there a deterministic Turing machine whose worst-case running time is $2^{o(n)}$ in
the input length $n$ and which, given a prime $p$, an irreducible polynomial $f$ over
$\mathbb{F}_p$, an elliptic curve $E$ over the finite field $\mathbb{F}_p[X]/(f)$, and points
$P, Q \in E$ with $Q$ in the subgroup generated by $P$, outputs a natural number $k$ with
$Q = kP$?

Here $2^{o(n)}$ means: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ the running time on inputs of length $n$ is at
most $2^{\varepsilon n}$ for all large $n$. The machine may output anything on inputs that do not
describe such an instance.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11 14 68]
theorem discrete_logarithm_2 :
    answer(sorry) ↔
      ∃ (dlog : List ℕ → ℕ)
        (M : TM2ComputableInTime finEncodingListNat finEncodingNatBool dlog),
        IsSubexponential M.time ∧
        ∀ (I : Input) [Fact I.p.Prime] [Fact (Irreducible I.modulus)] [I.curve.IsElliptic]
          (P Q : I.curve.toAffine.Point), I.IsPoint I.P P → I.IsPoint I.Q Q →
          Q ∈ AddSubgroup.zmultiples P → dlog I.encode • P = Q := by
  sorry

end DiscreteLogarithm2
attempts.decomposition_objections: None. The single-slot decomposition is right. The notes correctly flag the two conventions (deterministic vs randomized, computation model) that had to be fixed; I chose deterministic worst-case TM2 machines (Mathlib's only complexity framework) and record that the randomized reading is not covered. The bespoke definitions IsSubexponential and finEncodingListNat are reusable and would belong in FormalConjecturesForMathlib under the repo's rules; they are kept in the problem file only because the task allows a single output file.
modeling_decisions: Computation model: deterministic multi-stack Turing machine (`Turing.FinTM2` / `TM2ComputableInTime`, as in Millenium/PvsNP.lean), worst-case running time as a function of encoded input length. Randomized (expected or bounded-error) algorithms are NOT modeled: Mathlib has no probabilistic machine, and a clean randomized formulation would require per-input step bounds outside `TM2ComputableInTime`. A randomized-only sub-exponential algorithm would answer the informal question positively but would not by itself make this formal statement true; the docstring says 'deterministic' explicitly.

Sub-exponential := 2^{o(n)} (`IsSubexponential t := ∀ ε > 0, eventually t n ≤ 2^(ε n)`, real rpow). This is the meaning standard in the discrete-log/factoring literature (index calculus L_q[1/2], NFS L_q[1/3] are sub-exponential in this sense); the alternative class SUBEXP = ∩_ε DTIME(2^{n^ε}) would exclude those and was not chosen.

n is the length of the encoded input string. For reduced representations n = Θ(log q) (between log₂ q and about 8 log₂ q + 13), so 2^{o(n)} is equivalent to 2^{o(log q)}; the notes' 'n ≈ log field size' is honoured up to a constant factor, which 2^{o(n)} is robust against.

Finite fields are given concretely as 𝔽_p[X]/(f) = `AdjoinRoot` of the polynomial whose base-p digits are the natural number `I.f`, with `Fact p.Prime` and `Fact (Irreducible f)` as hypotheses; every finite field arises (up to isomorphism) this way, and all irreducible f (all representations) must be handled. Field elements are naturals whose base-p digits are the coefficients of a polynomial in the root (`Nat.ofDigits (AdjoinRoot.root f) (Nat.digits p c)`); non-reduced representatives (c ≥ p^deg f) are allowed as inputs, which only strengthens the requirement trivially (poly-time reduction).

Curve given in general Weierstrass form (a₁,a₂,a₃,a₄,a₆) so characteristic 2 and 3 are covered; `[I.curve.IsElliptic]` (Δ a unit, i.e. Δ ≠ 0 over a field) is a hypothesis, so singular cubics are excluded as the statement says 'elliptic curve'.

Points are `Option (ℕ × ℕ)` (none = point at infinity), related to Mathlib points by `Input.IsPoint` (`P = 0` resp. `∃ h : Nonsingular (elem x) (elem y), P = .some h`). Q ∈ ⟨P⟩ is `Q ∈ AddSubgroup.zmultiples P`; the output is a natural k with `k • P = Q` (ℕ-smul; suffices since the group is finite, and the discrete log is only defined modulo the order of P).

The machine must be total on all of `List ℕ` (required by `TM2ComputableInTime`); on lists that do not encode a valid instance its output is unconstrained. Real algorithms satisfy this by adding a clock.

Instance-implicit binders `∀ (I : Input) [Fact I.p.Prime] [Fact (Irreducible I.modulus)] [I.curve.IsElliptic]` inside the ∃ are used to obtain the Field and group instances; `open scoped Classical in` supplies `DecidableEq` for the point group law.

$P, Q \in E$ with $Q$ in the subgroup generated by $P$, outputs a natural number $k$ with
$Q = kP$?

describe such an instance.
-/

    answer(sorry) ↔
      ∃ (dlog : List ℕ → ℕ)
        (M : TM2ComputableInTime finEncodingListNat finEncodingNatBool dlog),
        IsSubexponential M.time ∧
        ∀ (I : Input) [Fact I.p.Prime] [Fact (Irreducible I.modulus)] [I.curve.IsElliptic]
          (P Q : I.curve.toAffine.Point), I.IsPoint I.P P → I.IsPoint I.Q Q →

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# The elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem in subexponential time

Let $E$ be an elliptic curve over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$, let $P \in E(\mathbb{F}_q)$
and let $Q$ be in the cyclic subgroup generated by $P$. The *discrete logarithm problem* on $E$
asks for an integer $k$ with $Q = kP$. The best known classical algorithms for a general elliptic
curve (baby-step giant-step, Pollard's rho) run in time about $\sqrt{q} = 2^{\Theta(\log q)}$,
which is exponential in the input size $\Theta(\log q)$.

Wikipedia asks: *Can a discrete logarithm on an elliptic curve be computed in sub-exponential
time?*

We formalise this as the existence of a deterministic Turing machine (the `TM2` model of
`Mathlib.Computability.TMComputable`, as in `FormalConjectures/Millenium/PvsNP.lean`) that
solves the discrete logarithm problem on every elliptic curve over every finite field within
$2^{o(n)}$ steps, where $n$ is the length of the input. Finite fields are presented as
$\mathbb{F}_p[X]/(f)$ with $f$ monic irreducible, curves by a Weierstrass equation, and the input
is a fixed binary encoding of all this data, so that $n = \Theta(\log q)$.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Discrete logarithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/discrete_logarithm)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [Wikipedia, Elliptic-curve cryptography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic-curve_cryptography)
-/

open Computability Turing Polynomial Filter

namespace DiscreteLogarithm2

/--
An input to the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem. It consists of
- a prime `p`,
- a monic irreducible polynomial `f` over `𝔽_p = ZMod p`, presenting the finite field
  `𝔽_q = 𝔽_p[X]/(f) = AdjoinRoot f` with `q = p ^ deg f`,
- an elliptic curve `E` over `𝔽_q`, given by a (long) Weierstrass equation,
- two points `P` and `Q` of `E(𝔽_q)`.

Every finite field, and every elliptic curve over it, arises this way up to isomorphism.
-/
structure Input where
  /-- The characteristic of the finite field. -/
  p : ℕ
  [hp : Fact p.Prime]
  /-- The monic irreducible polynomial `f` presenting the finite field `𝔽_p[X]/(f)`. -/
  f : (ZMod p)[X]
  monic : f.Monic
  [irreducible : Fact (Irreducible f)]
  /-- The elliptic curve, given by a Weierstrass equation over `𝔽_p[X]/(f)`. -/
  E : WeierstrassCurve (AdjoinRoot f)
  [elliptic : E.IsElliptic]
  /-- The base point. -/
  P : E.toAffine.Point
  /-- The point whose discrete logarithm with respect to `P` is sought. -/
  Q : E.toAffine.Point

attribute [instance] Input.hp Input.irreducible Input.elliptic

namespace Input

variable (I : Input)

/--
The list of the `deg f` coefficients, as natural numbers `< p`, of the unique representative of
degree `< deg f` of an element of `𝔽_p[X]/(f)`.
-/
noncomputable def encodeElem (x : AdjoinRoot I.f) : List ℕ :=
  (List.range I.f.natDegree).map fun i => ((AdjoinRoot.modByMonicHom I.monic x).coeff i).val

/--
A point of `E(𝔽_q)` is encoded by the tag `0` if it is the point at infinity, and by the tag `1`
followed by the encodings of its two affine coordinates otherwise.
-/
noncomputable def encodePoint : I.E.toAffine.Point → List ℕ
  | .zero => [0]
  | .some (x := x) (y := y) _ => 1 :: (I.encodeElem x ++ I.encodeElem y)

/--
The list of natural numbers describing an input: the prime `p`, the degree `n` of `f`, the `n`
lower coefficients of `f` (the leading coefficient is `1`), the coefficients `a₁, a₂, a₃, a₄, a₆`
of the Weierstrass equation of `E`, and the two points `P` and `Q`.
-/
noncomputable def toNatList : List ℕ :=
  [I.p, I.f.natDegree] ++ (List.range I.f.natDegree).map (fun i => (I.f.coeff i).val) ++
    I.encodeElem I.E.a₁ ++ I.encodeElem I.E.a₂ ++ I.encodeElem I.E.a₃ ++ I.encodeElem I.E.a₄ ++
    I.encodeElem I.E.a₆ ++ I.encodePoint I.P ++ I.encodePoint I.Q

end Input

/--
A list of natural numbers is written over the standard Turing machine alphabet `Γ'` by writing
each number in binary (via `Computability.encodeNat`, least significant bit first) followed by a
`comma`.
-/
def encodeNatList (l : List ℕ) : List Γ' :=
  (l.map fun k => (encodeNat k).map Γ'.bit ++ [Γ'.comma]).flatten

/-- The binary encoding of an input, over the alphabet `Γ'`. Its length is `Θ(log q)`. -/
noncomputable def Input.encode (I : Input) : List Γ' :=
  encodeNatList I.toNatList

/--
A time bound `T : ℕ → ℕ` is *subexponential* if `T n = 2 ^ o(n)`, that is, if for every
`ε > 0` we have `T n ≤ 2 ^ (ε * n)` for all sufficiently large `n`.
-/
def IsSubexponential (T : ℕ → ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop, (T n : ℝ) ≤ 2 ^ (ε * n)

/--
**Elliptic curve discrete logarithms in subexponential time.**

Can a discrete logarithm on an elliptic curve be computed in sub-exponential time?

That is, is there a deterministic Turing machine `M` and a subexponential time bound
`T n = 2 ^ o(n)` such that for every prime `p`, every finite field `𝔽_q = 𝔽_p[X]/(f)` with `f`
monic irreducible, every elliptic curve `E` over `𝔽_q` given by a Weierstrass equation and all
points `P`, `Q` of `E(𝔽_q)` with `Q` in the subgroup generated by `P`, the machine `M`, started
on the binary encoding of `(p, f, E, P, Q)`, halts within `T (input length)` steps and outputs
the binary encoding of a natural number `k` with `Q = k • P`?

The input length is `Θ(log q)`, so the generic algorithms, which take about `√q` steps, are
exponential. Only the worst-case running time of deterministic (classical) machines is
considered; Shor's algorithm solves the problem in polynomial time on a quantum computer.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11 14 68]
theorem discrete_logarithm_2 :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ (M : TM2ComputableAux Γ' Γ') (T : ℕ → ℕ), IsSubexponential T ∧
      ∀ I : Input, (∃ k : ℕ, I.Q = k • I.P) → ∃ k : ℕ, I.Q = k • I.P ∧
        Nonempty (TM2OutputsInTime M.tm (I.encode.map M.inputAlphabet.symm)
          (some (((encodeNat k).map Γ'.bit).map M.outputAlphabet.symm)) (T I.encode.length)) := by
  sorry

/-- The point at infinity is encoded by the single tag `0`. -/
@[category test, AMS 11 14 68]
theorem Input.encodePoint_zero (I : Input) : I.encodePoint 0 = [0] :=
  rfl

/-- The list `[0, 1, 2]` is encoded as `, 1 , 01 ,` (least significant bit first). -/
@[category test, AMS 68]
theorem encodeNatList_example :
    encodeNatList [0, 1, 2] = [.comma, .bit true, .comma, .bit false, .bit true, .comma] := by
  have h2 : (2 : ℕ) = ((Num.pos (PosNum.bit0 1) : Num) : ℕ) := rfl
  have h1 : (1 : ℕ) = ((Num.pos 1 : Num) : ℕ) := rfl
  have h0 : (0 : ℕ) = ((Num.zero : Num) : ℕ) := rfl
  simp only [encodeNatList, List.map_cons, List.map_nil, encodeNat, h2, h1, h0, Num.of_to_nat]
  rfl

/-- Polynomial time bounds are subexponential. -/
@[category test, AMS 68]
theorem isSubexponential_pow (d : ℕ) : IsSubexponential fun n => n ^ d := by
  intro ε hε
  have h := isLittleO_pow_exp_pos_mul_atTop d (mul_pos hε (Real.log_pos one_lt_two))
  filter_upwards [tendsto_natCast_atTop_atTop.eventually (h.bound one_pos)] with n hn
  simp only [Real.norm_eq_abs, one_mul, abs_pow, Nat.abs_cast] at hn
  push_cast
  calc (n : ℝ) ^ d ≤ |Real.exp (ε * Real.log 2 * n)| := hn
    _ = 2 ^ (ε * n) := by
      rw [abs_of_pos (Real.exp_pos _), Real.rpow_def_of_pos two_pos]
      ring_nf

/-- The exponential time bound `2 ^ n` is not subexponential. -/
@[category test, AMS 68]
theorem not_isSubexponential_two_pow : ¬ IsSubexponential fun n => 2 ^ n := by
  intro h
  obtain ⟨N, hN⟩ := (h (1 / 2) (by norm_num)).exists_forall_of_atTop
  have h1 := hN (N + 1) (by omega)
  have h2 : ((2 : ℝ) ^ ((1 / 2 : ℝ) * ((N + 1 : ℕ) : ℝ))) < 2 ^ ((N + 1 : ℕ) : ℝ) :=
    Real.rpow_lt_rpow_of_exponent_lt one_lt_two (by push_cast; linarith)
  rw [Real.rpow_natCast] at h2
  push_cast at h1 h2
  linarith

end DiscreteLogarithm2

As the table's notes anticipate, the conventions (deterministic vs randomized, computation model, exact meaning of subexponential, input encoding) had to be fixed; they are recorded in modeling_decisions and in the theorem docstring. The randomized-algorithm reading could not be offered as a variant because no probabilistic computation primitives exist in Mathlib.
modeling_decisions: Computation model: deterministic Turing machines in Mathlib's `TM2` model (`Turing.FinTM2`, `TM2OutputsInTime`), bundled with alphabet equivalences via `TM2ComputableAux Γ' Γ'`, exactly as `FormalConjectures/Millenium/PvsNP.lean` does. Randomized (Las Vegas / expected-time) algorithms, which the cryptographic literature often allows, are NOT modelled: Mathlib has no probabilistic TM primitives. This is recorded in the theorem docstring; a randomized variant is a distinct question.

Sub-exponential time is taken in the standard complexity-theoretic sense `T(n) = 2^{o(n)}`: `∀ ε > 0, T n ≤ 2^(ε n)` for all large `n` (definition `IsSubexponential`). This is the sense used for factoring/DLP (e.g. L_q[α, c] with α < 1 is 2^{o(n)}); the stricter alternative `∀ ε, T n ≤ 2^{n^ε}` was not used. One uniform machine with one bound `T` is required (not one machine per ε).

Input size: the time bound is in the length of a fixed concrete encoding `Input.encode` over Mathlib's alphabet `Γ'`: the numbers p, deg f, the deg f lower coefficients of f, the five Weierstrass coefficients a₁,a₂,a₃,a₄,a₆ and the two points (tag 0 for the point at infinity, tag 1 followed by both coordinates otherwise), each number written in binary (`Computability.encodeNat`) followed by a comma; field elements are written via their canonical representative of degree < deg f (`AdjoinRoot.modByMonicHom`). The encoding is injective and of length Θ(log q); it contains only the instance data (no leak of k). Injectivity is not formally proved (it is not needed to state the problem, since `TM2OutputsInTime` is used directly rather than `TM2ComputableInTime` with a `FinEncoding`).

Finite fields: every finite field is presented as `AdjoinRoot f` with `f : (ZMod p)[X]` monic and irreducible, `p` prime (`Fact p.Prime`, `Fact (Irreducible f)` as instance fields). This covers all finite fields 𝔽_{p^n} (with n ≥ 1 automatic from irreducibility) up to isomorphism; restricting to monic `f` is without loss of generality over a field and is needed for the canonical representatives.

Elliptic curves: `WeierstrassCurve` with `[E.IsElliptic]` (nonsingular), i.e. a long Weierstrass equation, so characteristic 2 and 3 are covered; the group is Mathlib's `E.toAffine.Point` with its `AddCommGroup` structure. Every elliptic curve over a field is isomorphic to such a curve.

Discrete logarithm problem is stated as a promise problem: the machine is only constrained on inputs with `∃ k : ℕ, Q = k • P` (equivalently `Q ∈ zmultiples P` in the finite group); it may output any natural number `k` with `Q = k • P` (not necessarily reduced modulo the order of `P`), written in binary; the output must be exactly the canonical binary string (`encodeNat k`, least significant bit first) on the output stack, following Mathlib's `TM2ComputableInTime` convention.

`answer(True)` means a subexponential (classical, deterministic) algorithm exists; `answer(False)` means none exists. Brute force / generic algorithms take 2^{Θ(n)} steps so the statement is not trivially true; the `Input` type is nonempty and the encoding is injective so it is not trivially false.

/-!
# Elliptic-curve discrete logarithms

Can elliptic-curve discrete logarithms over arbitrary finite fields be computed in
sub-exponential time on a classical computer?

*References:*

- [Wikipedia, Discrete logarithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/discrete_logarithm)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)

open Asymptotics Computability Turing

namespace DiscreteLogarithm2

/-- A self-delimiting bit encoding of a natural number. -/
def natCode (n : ℕ) : List Bool :=
  let bits := Computability.encodeNat n
  List.replicate bits.length false ++ true :: bits

/-- Concatenate self-delimiting encodings of a list of natural numbers. -/
def natListCode (l : List ℕ) : List Bool :=
  l.flatMap natCode

/-- The coordinates of `x` in the power basis `b`, represented by their standard residues
modulo `p`. -/
noncomputable def coordinateCode {p : ℕ} {F : Type*} [Field F] [Algebra (ZMod p) F]
    (b : PowerBasis (ZMod p) F) (x : F) : List ℕ :=
  List.ofFn fun i ↦ (b.basis.repr x i).val

/-- A coordinate encoding of an affine elliptic-curve point, with `0` representing the point at
infinity and `1` introducing the two affine coordinates. -/
noncomputable def pointCode {p : ℕ} {F : Type*} [Field F] [Algebra (ZMod p) F]
    (b : PowerBasis (ZMod p) F) {E : WeierstrassCurve F} : E.toAffine.Point → List ℕ
  | .zero => [0]
  | .some (x := x) (y := y) _ =>
      1 :: coordinateCode b x ++ coordinateCode b y

/-- A bit encoding of an elliptic-curve discrete-logarithm instance over a finite field. The field
is presented by its characteristic and the minimal polynomial of a power-basis generator. The rest
of the code contains the five Weierstrass coefficients and the two points in that basis. -/
noncomputable def inputCode {p : ℕ} {F : Type*} [Field F] [Algebra (ZMod p) F]
    (b : PowerBasis (ZMod p) F) (E : WeierstrassCurve F)
    (P Q : E.toAffine.Point) : List Bool :=
  natListCode <|
    p :: b.dim ::
    (List.range (b.dim + 1)).map (fun i ↦ (b.minpolyGen.coeff i).val) ++
    coordinateCode b E.a₁ ++ coordinateCode b E.a₂ ++ coordinateCode b E.a₃ ++
    coordinateCode b E.a₄ ++ coordinateCode b E.a₆ ++ pointCode b P ++ pointCode b Q

/--
Can a discrete logarithm on an elliptic curve be computed in sub-exponential time?

Precisely, this asks for one deterministic classical multi-tape Turing machine which works for
every elliptic curve over every finite field. A finite field of characteristic $p$ and degree $d$
is supplied by the minimal polynomial of a power-basis generator over $\mathbb F_p$. Given points $P,Q$
with $Q\in\langle P\rangle$, the machine must output a natural number $k$ such that $Q=kP$.
The worst-case step bound $T(n)$ is sub-exponential in the bit-length $n$ of this encoding, meaning
$\log T(n)=o(n)$. This formulation fixes the classical machine model and uses deterministic
worst-case, rather than randomized expected, running time.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11 68]
theorem discrete_logarithm_2 :
    answer(sorry) ↔
      ∃ (M : TM2ComputableAux Bool Bool) (T : ℕ → ℕ),
        (fun n : ℕ ↦ Real.log (T n : ℝ)) =o[atTop] (fun n : ℕ ↦ (n : ℝ)) ∧
        ∀ (p : ℕ) (F : Type) [Field F] [Fintype F] [DecidableEq F] [CharP F p]
          [Algebra (ZMod p) F] (_hp : p.Prime) (b : PowerBasis (ZMod p) F)
          (E : WeierstrassCurve F) [E.IsElliptic] (P Q : E.toAffine.Point),
          (∃ k : ℕ, Q = k • P) →
            ∃ k : ℕ, Q = k • P ∧
              Nonempty (TM2OutputsInTime M.tm
                (List.map M.inputAlphabet.invFun (inputCode b E P Q))
                (some (List.map M.outputAlphabet.invFun (Computability.encodeNat k)))
                (T (inputCode b E P Q).length)) := by
  sorry

end DiscreteLogarithm2

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# The elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem

Let $E$ be an elliptic curve in Weierstrass form over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$, let $P$ be a
point of $E(\mathbb{F}_q)$ and let $Q$ be a point of the subgroup generated by $P$. The
**discrete logarithm problem** on $E$ asks for an integer $k$ with $Q = kP$.

The best known classical algorithms for a general elliptic curve (baby-step giant-step,
Pollard's rho) take time about $\sqrt{q}$, which is exponential in the input size
$n = \Theta(\log q)$. Sub-exponential algorithms are known only for special families of curves
(supersingular curves via the MOV attack, anomalous curves, ...), and Shor's algorithm solves the
problem in polynomial time on a quantum computer. Wikipedia lists the following question as open:

> Can a discrete logarithm on an elliptic curve be computed in sub-exponential time?

## Formalisation choices

- The computational model is the deterministic two-stack Turing machine `Turing.FinTM2` of
  Mathlib, as in `FormalConjectures.Millenium.PvsNP`. Randomised algorithms are not modelled.
- An algorithm is a total function `List ℕ → ℕ` computed by such a machine within `T n` steps on
  every input of length `n`, where `T` is sub-exponential: $\log T(n) = o(n)$, that is,
  $T(n) = 2^{o(n)}$.
- An instance is the list of naturals `[p, c, a₁, a₂, a₃, a₄, a₆, zP, xP, yP, zQ, xQ, yQ]`. It is
  encoded by writing each natural in binary and terminating it with a separator symbol.
  * `p` is the characteristic, a prime.
  * `c` describes the polynomial `f ∈ 𝔽_p[X]` whose coefficients are the base-`p` digits of `c`;
    `f` must be irreducible and the field is `𝔽_q = 𝔽_p[X] / (f)`. Every finite field arises in
    this way, prime fields included (take `f = X`, i.e. `c = p`).
  * every further natural `e` denotes the field element given by the polynomial whose
    coefficients are the base-`p` digits of `e`.
  * `a₁, a₂, a₃, a₄, a₆` are the Weierstrass coefficients of the curve, whose discriminant must
    be nonzero.
  * `(z, x, y)` denotes the point at infinity when `z = 0` and the affine point `(x, y)`
    otherwise.

  Every instance has a reduced representative in which all field elements are given by naturals
  smaller than `q`; its encoding has length $\Theta(\log q)$, so sub-exponential time in the
  input length is the same as time $q^{o(1)}$. Longer, non-reduced representatives of the same
  instance only give the algorithm more time.
- The algorithm is only required to be correct on well-formed instances with `Q ∈ ⟨P⟩`, but it
  must halt within the time bound on every input, as usual for promise problems.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia: Discrete logarithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/discrete_logarithm)
- [Wikipedia: List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [Wikipedia: Elliptic-curve cryptography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic-curve_cryptography)
-/

open Computability Filter Polynomial Turing WeierstrassCurve

namespace DiscreteLogarithm2

/-- Encoding of a list of naturals over the alphabet `Option Bool`: each natural is written in
binary (`Computability.encodeNat`) and is terminated by the separator `none`. -/
def finEncodingListNat : FinEncoding (List ℕ) where
  Γ := Option Bool
  encode l := l.flatMap fun n => (encodeNat n).map some ++ [none]
  decode l := some <| (l.splitOnP Option.isNone).dropLast.map fun w =>
    decodeNat (w.map fun b => b.getD false)
  decode_encode l := by
    congr 1
    induction l with
    | nil => simp
    | cons n l ih =>
      simp only [List.flatMap_cons, List.append_assoc, List.singleton_append] at ih ⊢
      rw [splitOnP_append_cons _ _ _ _ (by simp), splitOnP_isNone_map_some]
      rw [List.singleton_append, List.dropLast_cons_of_ne_nil (List.splitOnP_ne_nil _ _)]
      simpa [List.map_map, Function.comp_def] using ih
  ΓFin := inferInstance

/-- The encoding of `[2, 5]`: `2 = 10₂` and `5 = 101₂`, least significant bit first. -/
@[category test, AMS 68]
theorem finEncodingListNat_encode_example : finEncodingListNat.encode [2, 5] =
    [some false, some true, none, some true, some false, some true, none] := by
  unfold finEncodingListNat
  decide +kernel

/-- The length of the encoding of a list of naturals is the sum of the binary lengths of its
entries, plus one separator per entry. -/
@[category API, AMS 68]
theorem length_finEncodingListNat_encode (l : List ℕ) :
    (finEncodingListNat.encode l).length = (l.map fun n => (encodeNat n).length + 1).sum := by
  simp [finEncodingListNat, List.length_flatMap]

/-- A total function `f` is computable in sub-exponential time if some deterministic Turing
machine computes it within `T n` steps on every input of length `n`, where
$\log T(n) = o(n)$, i.e. $T(n) = 2^{o(n)}$. -/
def IsComputableInSubexponentialTime {α β : Type} (ea : FinEncoding α) (eb : FinEncoding β)
    (f : α → β) : Prop :=
  ∃ h : TM2ComputableInTime ea eb f,
    (fun n => Real.log (h.time n)) =o[atTop] fun n => (n : ℝ)

/-- The polynomial over `ZMod p` whose coefficients are the base-`p` digits of `e`
(Kronecker substitution). -/
noncomputable def polyOfNat (p e : ℕ) : (ZMod p)[X] :=
  ((Nat.digits p e).mapIdx fun i d => C (d : ZMod p) * X ^ i).sum

/-- `7 = 1 · 5 + 2`, so `7` describes the polynomial `2 + X` over `ZMod 5`. -/
@[category test, AMS 12]
theorem polyOfNat_example : polyOfNat 5 7 = C 2 + X := by
  simp [polyOfNat, List.mapIdx_cons]

/-- The natural `p` describes the polynomial `X` over `ZMod p`, so `𝔽_p[X] / (polyOfNat p p)` is
the prime field `𝔽_p` itself. -/
@[category API, AMS 12]
theorem polyOfNat_self {p : ℕ} (hp : 1 < p) : polyOfNat p p = X := by
  have h : Nat.digits p p = [0, 1] := by
    rw [Nat.digits_def' hp (by omega), Nat.mod_self, Nat.div_self (by omega),
      Nat.digits_of_lt p 1 one_ne_zero hp]
  simp [polyOfNat, h, List.mapIdx_cons]

/-- The element of `𝔽_p[X] / (polyOfNat p c)` represented by the natural number `e`. -/
noncomputable def fieldElem (p c e : ℕ) : AdjoinRoot (polyOfNat p c) :=
  AdjoinRoot.mk _ (polyOfNat p e)

/-- The Weierstrass curve over `𝔽_p[X] / (polyOfNat p c)` whose coefficients are represented by
the naturals `a₁, a₂, a₃, a₄, a₆`. -/
noncomputable def curve (p c a₁ a₂ a₃ a₄ a₆ : ℕ) : Affine (AdjoinRoot (polyOfNat p c)) where
  a₁ := fieldElem p c a₁
  a₂ := fieldElem p c a₂
  a₃ := fieldElem p c a₃
  a₄ := fieldElem p c a₄
  a₆ := fieldElem p c a₆

/-- The naturals `(z, x, y)` represent the point `P` of `W` if either `z = 0` and `P` is the
point at infinity, or `z ≠ 0` and `P` is the affine point whose coordinates are represented by
`x` and `y`. -/
def Represents {p c : ℕ} {W : Affine (AdjoinRoot (polyOfNat p c))} (z x y : ℕ) (P : W.Point) :
    Prop :=
  (z = 0 ∧ P = 0) ∨
    (z ≠ 0 ∧ ∃ h : W.Nonsingular (fieldElem p c x) (fieldElem p c y), P = Affine.Point.some h)

/-- Any triple `(0, x, y)` represents the point at infinity. -/
@[category test, AMS 14]
theorem represents_zero {p c : ℕ} {W : Affine (AdjoinRoot (polyOfNat p c))} (x y : ℕ) :
    Represents 0 x y (0 : W.Point) :=
  Or.inl ⟨rfl, rfl⟩

/--
**Elliptic curve discrete logarithm in sub-exponential time.**

Is there a deterministic classical algorithm which, given an elliptic curve $E$ over a finite
field $\mathbb{F}_q$, a point $P \in E(\mathbb{F}_q)$ and a point $Q \in \langle P \rangle$,
computes a natural number $k$ with $Q = kP$ in time $2^{o(n)}$, where $n$ is the length of the
input (so $n = \Theta(\log q)$ for reduced inputs)?

The field is given as $\mathbb{F}_p[X] / (f)$ with $p$ prime and $f$ irreducible, the curve by
its Weierstrass coefficients, and the points by their coordinates; see the module docstring for
the encoding. The algorithm must be correct for every elliptic curve over every finite field.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11 14 68]
theorem discrete_logarithm_2 :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ alg : List ℕ → ℕ,
      IsComputableInSubexponentialTime finEncodingListNat finEncodingNatBool alg ∧
      ∀ (p c a₁ a₂ a₃ a₄ a₆ zP xP yP zQ xQ yQ : ℕ) [Fact p.Prime]
        [Fact (Irreducible (polyOfNat p c))] [(curve p c a₁ a₂ a₃ a₄ a₆).IsElliptic]
        (P Q : (curve p c a₁ a₂ a₃ a₄ a₆).Point),
        Represents zP xP yP P → Represents zQ xQ yQ Q → Q ∈ AddSubgroup.zmultiples P →
        Q = alg [p, c, a₁, a₂, a₃, a₄, a₆, zP, xP, yP, zQ, xQ, yQ] • P := by
  sorry

end DiscreteLogarithm2

modeling_decisions: Computation model: deterministic two-stack Turing machine `Turing.FinTM2` / `TM2ComputableInTime` from Mathlib, following FormalConjectures/Millenium/PvsNP.lean. Randomised (Las Vegas / bounded-error / expected-time) algorithms, which the cryptanalytic literature usually admits, are NOT modelled: a positive answer via a randomised-only algorithm would not settle the formal statement. Modelling randomness faithfully is not possible with Mathlib's TM framework because its time bound is a function of the total input length, so random bits cannot be appended to the input without distorting the bound.

Sub-exponential time is taken to mean T(n) = 2^{o(n)}, formalised as `(fun n => Real.log (T n)) =o[atTop] (fun n => (n : ℝ))` (repo idiom, cf. ErdosProblems/1101.lean), where n is the length of the encoded input. `Real.log 0 = 0` is harmless: a bound of 0 steps only makes the machine's obligation harder.

Worst-case complexity: the machine must halt within `T(|w|)` steps on EVERY input w (including malformed ones and non-promise instances), the standard definition for promise problems (DTIME-style). Correctness is only required on well-formed instances with Q ∈ ⟨P⟩; on other inputs `alg` is unconstrained. The reviewer should confirm they accept this standard convention (an algorithm with a time-constructible bound on promise instances can always be clocked).

Finite field representation: 𝔽_q = 𝔽_p[X]/(f) as `AdjoinRoot (polyOfNat p c)` with `[Fact p.Prime]` and `[Fact (Irreducible (polyOfNat p c))]`; `polyOfNat p e` is the polynomial whose coefficients are the base-p digits of e (Kronecker substitution). Every finite field, including prime fields (c = p gives f = X, proven in `polyOfNat_self`), arises this way, and the field description is part of the input, so the algorithm must be uniform over all finite fields. Non-monic irreducible f is allowed (still a field).

Instance layout: the fixed list `[p, c, a₁, a₂, a₃, a₄, a₆, zP, xP, yP, zQ, xQ, yQ]` of naturals, encoded over the alphabet `Option Bool` by writing each natural in binary (Mathlib's `encodeNat`, LSB first) followed by a separator `none` (`finEncodingListNat`, with a proved `decode_encode`). For reduced representatives (field elements < q, z ∈ {0,1}) the encoding has length Θ(log q), so 2^{o(n)} = q^{o(1)}; non-reduced representatives (e ≥ q, huge z) are also valid inputs and merely give the algorithm more time (reduction mod f is polynomial), so they do not change the problem.

Points: `(z, x, y)` with z = 0 meaning the point at infinity (x, y ignored) and z ≠ 0 meaning the affine point (fieldElem x, fieldElem y); `Represents` requires a `Nonsingular` proof, which for an elliptic curve (Δ ≠ 0) is automatic for every point satisfying the Weierstrass equation. Points at infinity are included as inputs (trivial cases P = O or Q = O are covered, k = 0 works).
'Elliptic curve' is formalised as a long Weierstrass curve (a₁, a₂, a₃, a₄, a₆) with `WeierstrassCurve.IsElliptic` (IsUnit Δ, i.e. Δ ≠ 0 in the field); this covers characteristics 2 and 3.
